title: Part 2, Chapter 66
paragraphs: Which treats of what the reader will see, or what the listener will hear

As he left Barcelona, Don Quixote turned his gaze upon the spot where he had fallen. "Here Troy was," he said; "here my ill-luck, not my cowardice, robbed me of all the glory I had won; here Fortune made me the victim of her caprices; here the lustre of my achievements was dimmed; here, in a word, fell my happiness, never to rise again."

"Señor," said Sancho on hearing this, "it is the part of brave hearts to be patient in adversity just as much as to be glad in prosperity. I judge by myself: when I was a governor I was glad, and now that I am a squire and on foot I am not sad. And I have heard say that she whom people commonly call Fortune is a drunken whimsical jade, and, what is more, blind, and therefore neither sees what she does nor knows whom she casts down or whom she sets up."

"You are quite a philosopher, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "you speak very sensibly; I don't know who taught you. But I can tell you there is no such thing as Fortune in the world, nor does anything that takes place here, good or bad, come about by chance, but by the special preordination of heaven; and hence the common saying that 'each of us is the maker of his own Fortune.' I have been the maker of mine; but not with the proper amount of prudence, and my self-confidence has therefore made me pay dearly; for I should have reflected that Rocinante's feeble strength could not stand up to the mighty bulk of the Knight of the White Moon's horse. In a word, I ventured it, I did my best, I was overthrown — but though I lost my honour, I did not lose, nor can I lose, the virtue of keeping my word. When I was a knight-errant, daring and valiant, I backed my achievements by hand and deed; now that I am a humble squire I'll back my words by keeping the promise I have given. Forward then, Sancho my friend — let's go and keep the year of the novitiate in our own country, and in that seclusion we'll pick up fresh strength to return to my never-forgotten calling of arms."

"Señor," replied Sancho, "travelling on foot is not such a pleasant thing that it makes me feel disposed or tempted to make long marches. Let's leave this armour hung up on some tree, instead of somebody that's been hanged; and then with me on Dapple's back and my feet off the ground we'll arrange the stages as your worship pleases to measure them out. But to suppose I'm going to travel on foot, and make long stages at that, is to suppose nonsense."
"You say well, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "let my armour be hung up as a trophy, and under or around it we will carve on the trees what was inscribed on the trophy of Roland's armour —
_These let none move / Who dareth not his might with Roland prove._"
"That's the very thing," said Sancho; "and if it weren't that we should feel the want of Rocinante on the road, it would be just as well to leave him hung up too."
"And yet I'd rather not have either him or the armour hung up," said Don Quixote, "so it won't be said, 'for good service, a bad return.'"

"Your worship is right," said Sancho; "for, as sensible people hold, 'the fault of the ass must not be laid on the pack-saddle;' and since in this affair the fault is your worship's, punish yourself and don't let your anger break out against the already battered and bloody armour, or the meekness of Rocinante, or the tenderness of my feet, trying to make them travel more than is reasonable."

In conversation of this sort the whole of that day went by, as did the four following ones, without anything happening to interrupt their journey. But on the fifth, as they entered a village, they found a great many people at the door of an inn enjoying themselves, since it was a holiday. As Don Quixote approached, a peasant called out, "One of these two gentlemen who come here, and who don't know the parties, will tell us what we ought to do about our wager."
"That I will, certainly," said Don Quixote, "and according to the rights of the case, if I can manage to understand it."

"Well, here it is, worthy sir," said the peasant. "A man of this village who's so fat that he weighs twenty stone has challenged another, a neighbour of his, who weighs no more than nine, to run a race. The agreement was that they were to run a hundred paces with equal weights; and when the challenger was asked how the weights were to be equalised, he said that the other, weighing nine stone, should put eleven stone of iron on his back, so that the twenty stone of the thin man would equal the twenty stone of the fat one."

"Not at all," Sancho exclaimed at once, before Don Quixote could answer; "it's for me, who only a few days ago left off being a governor and a judge, as all the world knows, to settle these doubtful questions and give an opinion in disputes of every sort."
"Answer in God's name, Sancho my friend," said Don Quixote, "for I am not fit to give crumbs to a cat — my wits are so confused and upset."

With this permission, Sancho said to the peasants who stood clustered round him, waiting open-mouthed for the verdict, "Brothers, what the fat man is asking is not reasonable, nor has it a shadow of justice in it; because if it's true, as they say, that the challenged party may choose the weapons, the other has no right to choose ones that will prevent him from winning. My ruling, therefore, is this: that the fat challenger prune, peel, thin, trim, and correct himself, and take eleven stone of flesh off his body, here or there as he pleases and as suits him best; reduced in that way to nine stone weight, he'll make himself equal and even with his opponent's nine stone, and they'll be able to run on equal terms."

"By all that's good," said one of the peasants on hearing Sancho's decision, "the gentleman has spoken like a saint, and given judgment like a canon! But I'll bet the fat man won't part with an ounce of his flesh, let alone eleven stone."

"The best plan will be for them not to run," said another, "so that neither the thin man breaks down under the weight nor the fat one has to strip himself of his flesh. Let half the wager be spent on wine, and let's take these gentlemen to the tavern where there's the best, and 'over me be the cloak when it rains.'"

"I thank you, sirs," said Don Quixote, "but I can't stop for an instant, for sad thoughts and unhappy circumstances oblige me to seem discourteous and to travel fast." Spurring Rocinante, he pushed on, leaving them wondering at what they had seen and heard, at his own strange figure, and at the shrewdness of his servant — for such they took Sancho to be. Another of them observed, "If the servant is so clever, what must the master be? I'll bet, if they're going to Salamanca to study, they'll be alcaldes of the Court in no time; for it's a mere joke — only to read and read, have interest and good luck, and before a man knows where he is he finds himself with a staff in his hand or a mitre on his head."

That night master and man passed out in the open fields, and the next day, as they were continuing their journey, they saw coming towards them a man on foot with alforjas at his neck and a javelin or spiked staff in his hand — the very cut of a foot courier. As soon as he came close to Don Quixote he picked up his pace and, half running, came up to him, embraced his right thigh (for he could reach no higher), and exclaimed with evident pleasure, "O Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, what happiness it will be to my lord the duke's heart when he learns your worship is coming back to his castle — for he's still there with my lady the duchess!"
"I don't recognise you, friend," said Don Quixote, "and I don't know who you are unless you tell me."
"I am Tosilos, my lord the duke's lackey, Señor Don Quixote," replied the courier; "the one who refused to fight your worship about marrying the daughter of Doña Rodriguez."
"God bless me!" exclaimed Don Quixote; "is it possible you are the one whom my enemies the enchanters changed into the lackey you speak of, to rob me of the honour of that battle?"

"Nonsense, good sir!" said the messenger; "there was no enchantment or transformation at all. I entered the lists as lackey Tosilos and came out of them as lackey Tosilos. I thought I'd marry without fighting, since the girl had taken my fancy; but my scheme had a very different outcome, for as soon as your worship had left the castle my lord the duke had a hundred strokes of the stick given me for having gone against the orders he gave me before the combat. The upshot of the whole affair is that the girl has become a nun, Doña Rodriguez has gone back to Castile, and I'm now on my way to Barcelona with a packet of letters for the viceroy which my master is sending him. If your worship would like a drop, sound though warm, I have a gourd here full of the best, and some scraps of Tronchon cheese that'll serve as a provocative and wakener of your thirst if it happens to be asleep."
"I take the offer," said Sancho; "no more compliments about it; pour out, good Tosilos, in spite of all the enchanters in the Indies."

"You are indeed the greatest glutton in the world, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and the greatest fool on earth, not to be able to see that this courier is enchanted and this Tosilos a sham one. Stop with him and take your fill; I will go on slowly and wait for you to catch up."

The lackey laughed, unsheathed his gourd, unwalletted his scraps, and taking out a small loaf of bread, he and Sancho seated themselves on the green grass and in peace and good fellowship finished off the contents of the alforjas down to the bottom — so resolutely that they licked the wrapper of the letters, just because it smelt of cheese.
Said Tosilos to Sancho, "There's no doubt about it, Sancho my friend, this master of yours ought to be a madman."

"Ought!" said Sancho; "he owes no man anything; he pays for everything, especially when the coin is madness. I see it plain enough, and I tell him so plain enough; but what's the use? — especially now that it's all over with him, for here he is beaten by the Knight of the White Moon."

Tosilos begged him to explain what had happened, but Sancho replied that it wouldn't be good manners to leave his master waiting; some other day, if they met, there would be time enough for that. Then, getting up, after shaking out his doublet and brushing the crumbs out of his beard, he drove Dapple on before him, and saying goodbye to Tosilos, left him and rejoined his master, who was waiting for him under the shade of a tree.
